Chapter 4: The Cultural Roots of Fatphobia and Size Discrimination.
Picture a busy school cafeteria. There's a young girl who pauses before joining the others at lunch. She’s learned, in so many little ways, that her body makes her different. The jokes, the glances, the whispered remarks—they send a message that’s impossible to ignore: if you’re fat, it’s not just frowned upon, it’s somehow unacceptable. And this message? It’s everywhere. From TV shows and magazines to the games kids play on the playground.
But where did all this come from? The roots of fatphobia go way back—centuries, actually. Believe it or not, there was a time when bigger bodies were a sign of wealth and good health. But as societies changed, so did these ideas. By the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, being thin started to mean something different. Thinness became a symbol of self-control, discipline, even moral strength. In a world that was moving faster and demanding more productivity, these traits were put on a pedestal.
Imagine a factory worker, just trying to get by. She sees role models in newspapers and ads, and they’re always thin. The message is subtle, but it’s everywhere: if you want respect and success, you need to be slim. This connection between body size and character turns into a powerful way to sort people—deciding who’s worthy, and who isn’t.
Most of us don’t realize how much we’re influenced by these beliefs. The fear of being fat isn’t just about health—it's about status, identity, even a sense of belonging. People in larger bodies are often unfairly seen as lacking willpower, even though their size might have nothing to do with their choices. And this bias? It’s baked into our institutions—schools, workplaces, even healthcare.
The media plays a huge role in all of this. Think about it: how often do you see fat characters on TV or in movies in positive roles? When they do show up, they're usually the punchline or the ones we’re supposed to pity. Flip through a fashion magazine, and thinness is celebrated as the ultimate goal. Weight-loss ads? They promise love and acceptance, but only if you fit a certain mold.
Now, picture a college student who’s tired of feeling invisible. She starts to really look at the people she admires—her friends, her mentors, her family. And she realizes something: they come in every shape and size. It’s a moment of freedom, but also a little unsettling. If body size isn’t a true measure of someone’s worth, then maybe the whole system of judgment starts to fall apart.
The impact of fatphobia is huge. People in larger bodies face real discrimination—getting hired, finding housing, getting a fair shot at education. They’re more likely to be bullied, less likely to get good medical care, and often end up blaming themselves for the way they’re treated. The cost isn’t just missed opportunities—it’s lost confidence, lost joy, and lost connections.
So what’s really going on here? The fight against fatness isn’t just about health—it’s about power, prejudice, and deciding who gets to belong. The cultural roots of fatphobia are complex and deep. But here’s the thing: once we start to see them, we can finally begin to change them.
